## Effective self-help tips

* Being 20% more specific improves your results by 80%
* Ways to introduce specificity
  - Your own language
  - Narrow the scope, e.g., to a specific codebase
  - Use a tool with unique access to, e.g., a specific codebase
  - Commision a script to do something exhaustively
* Don't be shy to ask for receipts! E.g. show me where this appears in the codebase or the docs

## Talk like an expert {.center .smaller}

*Terence Tao discussing a surprising math result with ChatGPT*

> > It is remarkable that the jacobian is constant, that is an exceptional amount of cancellation. Does this polynomial map have any symmetry or other structure that makes this cancelation less miraculous?
>
> What stands out is the **shape** of the interaction. Tao starts his inquiry by noting a single, precise detail that intrigues him.

<small>[Code is the byproduct](https://yagmin.com/blog/code-is-the-byproduct/) — yagmin.com</small>

## Terse and precise {.center .smaller}

> Note what Tao is not doing.
>
> He is not building a rich contextual background for the LLM to unpack. He does not list his credentials or say, "you are a mathematical genius, make no mistakes."
>
> Instead, he is terse and precise. He asks narrow questions and gets narrow responses.
>
> Keep your requests narrow and specific. Let the output compound through repeated inquiries. Engage with the goal of improving your personal understanding.

<small>[Code is the byproduct](https://yagmin.com/blog/code-is-the-byproduct/) — yagmin.com</small>

## Agent: Create a Quarto document surveying `tools::R_user_dir()` usage {.smaller-title}

OK I'm not actually *doing* this one, but you could imagine directing an agent to:

* Enumerate all uses of `tools::R_user_dir()` in CRAN packages
* Create a raw report of GitHub permalinks to these call sites
* Analyze each call site re: how it's being used and when it was introduced
* Summarize the findings

## It's a great time to answer your own questions!

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}
* Chat: be as precise as your current understanding allows
* [GitHub search](https://github.com/search?type=code): [qualifiers](https://docs.github.com/en/search-github/github-code-search/understanding-github-code-search-syntax) are powerful, e.g.
  - `user:cran` searches across source of every CRAN package
  - `user:tidyverse` searches within the tidyverse organization
  - `path:*.yaml` search within YAML files
  - `repo:wch/r-source` searches the GitHub mirror of R's source
  - `language:R` searches R code
* [GitHub Chat with Copilot](https://github.com/copilot): knows about commits, issues, pull requests, in addition to code
* [DeepWiki](https://deepwiki.com): chat on top of an LLM-generated wiki for a codebase
:::

## Code is the byproduct of understanding {.center .smaller}

> How do you construct shared understanding? By narrowing the LLM's focus through domain-specific wording and keeping requests specific and cumulative.
>
> Tao pins ChatGPT to a "deep mathematics" headspace through terminology and the specificity of his question.
>
> If you don't understand something, set the stage for the LLM and it will capably fill in the missing 20%.

<small>[Code is the byproduct](https://yagmin.com/blog/code-is-the-byproduct/) — yagmin.com</small>

## DeepWiki {visibility="hidden"}

An LLM-generated wiki for a GitHub repo, plus a chat interface over it.

Take any repo URL and swap the domain:

* `github.com/posit-dev/positron`
* `deepwiki.com/posit-dev/positron`
